---
title: "Sequencers & Arpeggiators"
description: "Every kind of sequencer and arpeggiator as a small working instrument on one clock: arpeggiators, step and x0x grids, acid bass, analog knobs, conditional trigs, Euclidean, polymetric, Cartesian, Turing Machine, Markov, Game of Life, piano roll, tracker and loop recording. Play any two side by side."
toc: true
toc-depth: 2

Every sequencer answers the same two questions in its own way: **which note next** and **when**. This page has one of each
main kind, all running on the same clock, so you can hear them against each other. Hold a chord below, then press ▶ on any card,
or run two at once in *Compare two*. The cards that read the held chord are the arpeggiators and a few sequencers that follow
the chords; the rest use the key and scale.

## Input and tempo

::: {#sq-input}
:::

## Compare two

Pick any two kinds. They start together on the next beat, A in the left ear and B in the right, with their own controls.

::: {#sq-compare}
:::

## Arpeggiators

An arpeggiator needs a chord held down: it decides the **order** and the **rate**, you decide the notes.

::: {#sq-arp}
:::

## Step sequencers

You write each step by hand. The pattern loops exactly, except where a step carries a rule.

::: {#sq-step}
:::

## Pattern math

The pattern comes from a rule or a shape: spread hits evenly, let tracks of different lengths drift, walk a grid.

::: {#sq-math}
:::

## Generative

You set the odds; the machine picks the notes. Good for music that keeps changing without anyone touching it.

::: {#sq-gen}
:::

## Linear and recorded

No looping grid as the starting point: notes laid out in time, typed in rows, or played in and kept.

::: {#sq-linear}
:::

## Side-by-side table

Click a heading to sort, a family to filter, a name to jump to its card.

::: {#sq-table}
:::
